title: Forgive our mistakes
hook: the Ardas asks forgiveness for any letter added or missed, any slip in the reading

segments.voice: Yesterday, the petition, and your line: say why. Did one honest sentence change how you asked for something? Today, right after the reason is named, the Ardas does something humble. Day six hundred thirty-four.

Picture someone who has just finished reading the whole Guru Granth Sahib aloud. That's an akhand paath: about forty-eight hours of continuous reading, the readers taking turns through the night, more than fourteen hundred pages. At the end, the family stands for the Ardas. And somewhere in it comes a request that sounds almost like a proofreader's note. Forgive any letter added. Forgive any letter missed. Forgive every slip. After two days of care, the first thing asked is pardon for the mistakes.
screen: `FORTY-EIGHT HOURS OF READING.` → `MORE THAN 1,400 PAGES.` → `FORGIVE ANY LETTER MISSED.`

segments.voice: The Punjabi phrase is akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni. Akhar is a letter, a syllable. Vaadha is something added, ghaata something left out. Bhul is a mistake that comes from forgetting or not knowing. Chuk is a slip, a miss, like a hand that loses its grip. Maaf karni: please forgive. It's said after a reading, a recitation, a kirtan, any time the words of the Guru have passed through human mouths. Why would a letter matter so much? Because for Sikhs the Guru Granth Sahib is not a book about the Guru. It is the Guru, the living teacher in words. Reading it is something like speaking in the Guru's own voice, and care with every syllable is a form of respect. But the line is not anxious. It doesn't promise that the reading was perfect. It assumes it wasn't. Guru Nanak said as much in Sri Rag, on ang 61: everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator never do. That's not an insult to the readers. It's just the truth about people, said without drama. So the Ardas builds an apology into its own structure. Do your very best, then admit you probably fell short, then let it go and move on. There's freedom in that. A person who expects to be perfect freezes before starting. A person who knows forgiveness is part of the ritual can stand up, open the book, and begin. And notice the word is our. The readers ask together, for one another's slips as well as their own.
screen: `AKHAR: A LETTER, A SYLLABLE.` · `BHUL CHUK: FORGETTING, SLIPPING.` · `EVERYONE ERRS BUT THE GURU.` · `DO YOUR BEST, THEN ASK PARDON.` · then, large: `FORGIVE THE ERRORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: apologize once. Sit and think back over the last day or two. Let one small slip come up: a sharp word, a forgotten text, a promise that slid. Don't pile on more. One is enough. Notice how it feels in your body. Then picture saying sorry to that person in a single plain sentence, no excuses attached. If you pray, you can ask the One to forgive the errors, yours and theirs. When the sit ends, send that apology, or plan when you will. The bell holds the time.
Forgive our mistakes. Akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni: the Ardas asks pardon for any letter added or missed, any slip.
Your line: forgive the errors. Today, make one apology without a but in it. And when someone else slips, let one go without comment. Day six hundred thirty-four.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a mistake from forgetting, and a slip; said together, any error at all.

trapdoor: what you thought: a request to forgive big sins.
what it means: pardon for the small slips of reading and reciting, built into the prayer itself.
what a scholar hears: because the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru, exact recitation is a form of reverence; the formula pairs akhar vaadha ghaata (textual errors) with bhul chuk (human lapses).
